title: Main ideas and summaries
intro: Find the main point of the whole passage.

sections.heading: Use the screen to build a passage map
body: Give each paragraph a short job: introduce a problem, give evidence, explain a limit to a claim, or show a change. For a main-idea question, connect those jobs into one sentence about the whole passage.
Use the opening and ending as anchors, then check that your summary accounts for the middle. A topic such as “buses” is not yet a main idea.

examples.label: Worked method: Map paragraph jobs
examples.text:
The instrument maker placed a row of finished flutes in her window. Passersby saw smooth tubes; the apprentice saw the shavings swept away before opening.

He proposed displaying the shavings too. The maker asked what a heap would explain. He sorted pieces by the operations that had produced them and laid an unfinished flute beside the rows.

A visitor followed the sequence with one finger. The apprentice moved his name card away from the center so it would not interrupt the path.

Question:  Which paragraph map best captures the movement?
A. A finished product → an apprentice’s attempt to make it more decorative → a change in the shop’s prices
B. Different views of a product → a display that reveals the process → attention redirected toward that process
C. A maker’s objection → removal of the apprentice’s display → a visitor’s misunderstanding

Supported answer: Different views of a product → a display that reveals the process → attention redirected toward that process

Reason: The opening contrasts a finished object with its making; the middle organizes scraps into an explanation; the ending lets the visitor follow that sequence. The display does not change prices or disappear. Map the change in each paragraph’s role rather than treating an objection as the final outcome.

sections.heading: Find the controlling idea, not just the subject
body: Name the subject and what the passage develops about it. “A coating must keep its reflective surface to maintain performance” is a controlling claim; “roof coatings” is only a subject.
Test the claim against the opening, the major turn, and the ending. Preserve conditions and degree of certainty rather than assuming the strongest wording is the best summary.

examples.label: Worked method: Separate topic from controlling claim
examples.text:
Dark-colored roofs absorb much of the sunlight that strikes them. A reflective coating can reduce that absorbed energy, but its performance depends partly on what remains on the surface. Dust can cover the coating and alter its reflectance.

An engineer therefore compares both freshly coated and weathered panels. Her report treats reflectance as a property to maintain, not simply a number printed on a new product’s package.

Question: Which statement gives the controlling idea rather than only the subject?
A. The passage discusses reflective roof coatings.
B. Roof coatings should be selected entirely by the amount of dust nearby.
C. A coating’s cooling value depends on its continuing surface condition as well as its initial reflectance.

Supported answer: A coating’s cooling value depends on its continuing surface condition as well as its initial reflectance.

Reason: “Reflective roof coatings” names the subject but omits the development. The contrast between fresh and weathered panels supports a claim about maintained performance. Dust matters, but “entirely” discards the initial reflectance the passage also discusses. Build subject + what the writer establishes about it.

sections.heading: Match a summary to the passage’s full movement
body: Mark the argumentative turn: what did the writer or character expect, what complicated it, and what changed afterward? A summary should preserve that sequence without becoming a list of events.
Check the outcome against the middle. If the ending qualifies an earlier position, a choice that simply repeats the opening is incomplete.

examples.label: Worked method: Keep the argumentative turn
examples.text:
A school orchestra planned to perform an unfamiliar piece without an introduction, hoping listeners would encounter it without instructions about what to hear. During rehearsal, players disagreed about whether an abrupt silence was a joke or an interruption.

They recorded both versions and listened without the score. Neither sounded accidental. The conductor kept the silence but added a short spoken invitation to notice how the same pause might feel different on its return.

Question:  Which summary keeps the full movement?
A. An initial wish to avoid directing listeners becomes a more selective invitation to hear an unresolved musical possibility.
B. The orchestra resolves the disagreement by removing the ambiguous pause from the piece.
C. A conductor replaces the players’ experiment with a detailed explanation of the correct interpretation.

Supported answer: An initial wish to avoid directing listeners becomes a more selective invitation to hear an unresolved musical possibility.

Reason: The passage moves from no introduction through two workable readings to a selective prompt. The pause remains and no single correct reading is imposed. A summary should carry the starting position, the complication, and the limited revision rather than invent resolution by removal or instruction.

sections.heading: Reject narrow, inflated, and imported choices
body: Test three traps: a narrow choice covers only one detail; an inflated choice claims more than the passage; an imported choice adds an idea the text never develops.
Check who the answer includes and how sure it sounds. “The interviewed residents” is narrower than “everyone,” and “promising” is weaker than “proven.” Point to the words that support the choice.

examples.label: Worked method: Distinguish a true detail from the main idea
examples.text:
A city greenhouse opened early on two weekdays so gardeners could collect seedlings before work. The early visitors came in small numbers, but many said they could not attend the usual afternoon hours. Some used the service repeatedly.

The manager recommended keeping one early morning rather than two. That schedule preserved an option for the gardeners while concentrating the limited staff time.

Question: Which accurate-sounding summary is too narrow?
A. The manager adjusts an access service to balance a particular need with limited staffing.
B. Some gardeners collected seedlings before work.
C. A small early-morning program is retained in a form that requires less staff time.

Supported answer: Some gardeners collected seedlings before work.

Reason: The middle statement is a true event, but it omits both the access problem and the scheduling decision. The other summaries account for the need and the adjustment. A detail does not become the main idea merely because it is stated explicitly. Ask what important part of the passage would remain unexplained if your choice were the title.

sections.heading: Treat narrative change as evidence, not a slogan
body: Track an initial preference, a revealing action, and the final choice. Describe the change those actions support without inventing a permanent personality transformation.
Keep the remaining tension. A character can accept an inconvenience or revise one judgment while retaining earlier goals.

examples.label: Worked method: Infer narrative movement without inventing a moral
examples.text:
Tess always took the highest path above the beach. From there she could reach home without sand in her shoes. When her younger cousin visited, she agreed to walk beside the pools and carried his shoes along with her own.

He stopped at each patch of water. Tess first watched the time, then crouched to see what held him. At the steps home she brushed both pairs of feet clean. The next morning she asked him whether the pools would still be full after breakfast.

Question:  What change does the ending support?
A. Tess discovers that her cousin’s route is more efficient for reaching home.
B. Tess continues using the pools mainly to avoid disappointing her cousin.
C. Tess has developed an interest in a route she had previously avoided.

Supported answer: Tess has developed an interest in a route she had previously avoided.

Reason: The opening values the high path for avoiding sand. Crouching and asking about the next morning support a new interest, while cleaning feet preserves the inconvenience. The lower route is not established as more efficient, and the final invitation goes beyond merely accommodating a visitor.

sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: For a main-idea choice, check one sentence from the beginning and one from the ending. Then ask whether the middle supports the same movement.
If two choices remain, name their difference: who they include, how the writer feels, or what happens. Return to the part of the passage that settles that difference.

examples.label: Worked method: Settle two close summaries with a pivot
examples.text:
The curator’s draft called the restored dial “as its first owner saw it.” The conservator crossed out that phrase. The metal was original, but the hands had been replaced, and the lost glass was represented by a clear modern cover.

They kept the dial on display. The new caption named the surviving parts and distinguished them from the additions that made the object readable.

Question: Which detail separates “the restoration is rejected as inauthentic” from “the restoration is presented with its interventions made clear”?
A. The dial remains on display with additions identified.
B. The curator writes a first draft.
C. The dial once had an owner.

Supported answer: The dial remains on display with additions identified.

Reason: The two choices disagree about rejection versus qualified presentation. Keeping the object and identifying additions directly resolves that difference. Drafting and former ownership occur under either interpretation. When two summaries remain, locate the sentence on which their claims diverge instead of rereading every sentence equally.

sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: After a miss, label its cause: chose a detail, ignored the ending, exaggerated the conclusion, or imported an outside idea.
Rewrite the main idea in one sentence using two passage anchors. Then try a new passage; recognizing an answer you have already seen is not evidence of transfer.

examples.label: Worked method: Repair an overextended summary
examples.text:
A botanist’s notebook described a hillside in spring. Her later essay used those notes to explain how she learned the names of flowers along one route. She wrote that naming made some differences easier to notice, though she continued to encounter forms she could not identify.

A student summarized the essay as proof that learning names gives a complete understanding of nature.

Question: Which repair matches the stated experience?
A. Naming replaces the need to keep observing the hillside.
B. Learning names changes the botanist’s attention without ending what she has yet to learn.
C. The essay shows that unidentified flowers are less important than named ones.

Supported answer: Learning names changes the botanist’s attention without ending what she has yet to learn.

Reason: “Complete understanding” conflicts with the continuing unidentified forms. A repaired summary retains the positive change—easier noticing—while removing the unsupported completion claim. Neither replacing observation nor ranking flowers is supported. The useful repair names the exact overreach and keeps the evidence the mistaken answer began with.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The passage’s main idea is that the restoration:
choices: refuses every change to the original building
proves photographs make all demolition harmless
focuses exclusively on increasing ticket prices
combines practical safety changes with attention to historical evidence
check.explanation: Both safe access and preserved or documented history are emphasized; neither aim displaces the other. The supported answer is “combines practical safety changes with attention to historical evidence.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: During a restoration, the town replaced unsafe stairs but preserved the old doorway and photographed each change. The project’s report described the building as usable again without treating its history as an obstacle.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The passage primarily traces Ravi’s discovery that:
choices: questions prevent anyone from repairing objects
radios are simpler than every other device
learning repair can involve shared uncertainty and experimentation
experts never make mistakes
check.explanation: His initial image changes after seeing collaborative trial and error, and he returns ready to participate. The supported answer is “learning repair can involve shared uncertainty and experimentation.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Ravi expected the repair club to be a place where experts worked silently. Instead, members asked one another questions, tried solutions that failed, and laughed about familiar mistakes. He returned the following week with a broken radio and a list of questions.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The best summary is that organizers:
choices: cancel the park because outdoor festivals are unpopular
use an initial survey while seeking evidence from a broader group
discard every response as dishonest
have established every resident’s preferences
check.explanation: The group retains useful limited evidence and expands the inquiry rather than claiming complete representation. The supported answer is “use an initial survey while seeking evidence from a broader group.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: A survey showed interest in a new park, but responses came mainly from people attending an outdoor festival. Organizers kept the results, labeled the respondent group, and sought additional views before choosing facilities.

title: Details, sequence, and cause
intro: Find the exact detail that answers the question.

sections.heading: Use the screen to build a passage map
body: Map where each fact lives: people, events, dates, measurements, and explanations. You need locations, not a memorized list of details.
Use the question’s distinctive noun or action to return to the right paragraph. Read the neighboring sentence before choosing.

examples.label: Worked method: Map where a requested fact lives
examples.text:
The island clinic sends supply orders on Mondays. A coastal office checks the orders on Tuesdays and combines them into one shipment. The ferry carries the boxes on Thursday unless weather closes the harbor.

Urgent medicine travels by a different arrangement; it does not wait for the weekly supply shipment.

Question: To find when routine supplies are physically transported, which part should you use?
A. The sentence about Monday orders
B. The exception for urgent medicine
C. The Thursday ferry sentence and its weather condition

Supported answer: The Thursday ferry sentence and its weather condition

Reason: The requested action is transport, not ordering or checking. Thursday supplies the time and the harbor exception qualifies it. Monday belongs to a different action, and urgent medicine is outside “routine supplies.” A location map connects each date to its own event before matching an answer.

sections.heading: Turn the stem into a precise search
body: Turn the question into a search target: who did what, when, or under which condition? Find that event, then match the requested detail.
A correct quotation can still answer the wrong question. Check the actor, time, and unit before accepting a choice.

examples.label: Worked method: Locate actor, action, and condition
examples.text:
Before opening the workshop, Ada tested the repaired lamp using a new bulb. The bulb lit, but the switch jammed on its second use. She set the lamp on a marked shelf and recorded the fault. Only after replacing the switch did she call its owner.

Question: When did Ada contact the owner?
A. After replacing the faulty switch
B. Immediately after the new bulb lit
C. When she first placed the lamp on the marked shelf

Supported answer: After replacing the faulty switch

Reason: The phrase “Only after replacing the switch” attaches directly to calling the owner. The bulb test and marked shelf are earlier real events, which makes them tempting. Match the question’s action—contacting—not simply the first successful test.

sections.heading: Separate sequence from cause
body: Separate what happened next from what caused it. “Returns improved after reminders began” states sequence; it does not isolate reminders as the cause.
If the question asks why, find the explanation the text supplies. Do not replace it with a plausible explanation of your own.

examples.label: Worked method: Read a stated cause without promoting sequence
examples.text:
A hall’s new entrance opened in September. Concert attendance rose in October, when the orchestra also began offering cheaper afternoon tickets. The hall manager attributed the rise to the ticket offer, based on answers collected from returning patrons. She said the entrance had made arrivals smoother but had not been the reason those patrons booked.

Question: Which explanation does the passage attribute to the manager?
A. The entrance caused the rise because it opened first.
B. The ticket offer prompted the reported patrons to book.
C. The entrance and tickets had equal effects on booking.

Supported answer: The ticket offer prompted the reported patrons to book.

Reason: The manager’s stated explanation concerns the ticket offer and the surveyed patrons. The entrance opening is earlier, but sequence alone does not make it her asserted cause. No equal division of effects is reported. A detail question can ask what a speaker says even when the passage is not proving that speaker’s account universally.

sections.heading: Control the unit, speaker, and condition
body: Keep the number attached to what it counts. Tool returns are not unique borrowers; occupied seats are not distinct visitors.
Check speaker and condition too. A volunteer’s claim is not automatically the author’s conclusion, and results for one group do not describe everyone.

examples.label: Worked method: Keep a number attached to its denominator
examples.text:
The repair desk logged 36 visits involving 24 customers in one week. Nine visits were follow-ups on earlier work. The coordinator reported visits and customers in separate columns because one customer could return more than once.

Question: Which statement preserves the recorded quantity?
A. Thirty-six customers had items repaired.
B. Nine of the customers visited only for follow-up work.
C. The desk recorded thirty-six visits, some made by returning customers.

Supported answer: The desk recorded thirty-six visits, some made by returning customers.

Reason: Thirty-six counts visits, not unique customers. Nine also counts visits; it does not identify nine distinct people or establish their only reason for attending. The separate customer count is 24. Keep each value paired with its unit before paraphrasing it.

sections.heading: Check a paraphrase without demanding identical wording
body: A correct paraphrase keeps the fact and its strength while changing the wording. “Guarded support” can become “cautious approval”; it cannot become “proof.”
Substitute the choice into the passage’s claim. Reject a choice that copies familiar words but changes their relationship.

examples.label: Worked method: Preserve the strength of a paraphrase
examples.text:
The astronomer called the dimming pattern “compatible with a passing object” but noted that a change in the star itself had not been excluded. The report recommended observing another event before favoring either explanation.

Question: Which paraphrase is faithful?
A. A passing object remains a possible explanation, while an alternative still needs testing.
B. The pattern establishes that a passing object caused the dimming.
C. The report favors a change in the star over a passing object.

Supported answer: A passing object remains a possible explanation, while an alternative still needs testing.

Reason: “Compatible with” allows a passing object without selecting it as the cause. “Had not been excluded” preserves a stellar alternative, and the next observation is meant to help decide. Establishing one cause or favoring the other changes the report’s stated certainty.

sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: Find the requested fact before weighing all the choices. Mark the sentence that answers the precise question.
When two options differ by a date, person, or condition, compare that feature directly with the source. Avoid rereading unrelated paragraphs.

examples.label: Worked method: Discriminate between adjacent dates
examples.text:
The committee approved the design in March and sent it for a safety review. Inspectors returned comments in April. The builder revised the railing in May, and the committee approved that revision in June. Work on the site began in July.

Question: Which date answers when the revised railing received approval?
A. May
B. June
C. July

Supported answer: June

Reason: May is when the builder changed the railing; June is when the committee approved that change; July is the start of construction. All are relevant to the project, but only June matches both “revised railing” and “approval.” Checking those two features is faster and safer than choosing the nearest remembered date.

sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: Identify the exact mismatch in a missed detail: wrong speaker, unit, date, condition, or cause.
Write the corrected fact with its limits intact: who, when, how many, or under what conditions. Then try that same check on a fresh passage.

examples.label: Worked method: Repair a speaker-and-scope error
examples.text:
The organizer predicted that the evening session would help all participants. After the first session, three attendees said its timing suited them; two other attendees did not submit comments. The report quoted the favorable comments but made no statement about the two who had not responded.

Question: How should “the report confirms that everyone preferred the evening” be corrected?
A. The organizer’s prediction is proved because favorable comments were received.
B. The two silent attendees opposed the timing.
C. Three attendees reported favorable timing; the other attendees’ views were not recorded.

Supported answer: Three attendees reported favorable timing; the other attendees’ views were not recorded.

Reason: The original prediction belongs to the organizer, while the report contains three comments and two unknown responses. Neither support nor opposition can be assigned to silent attendees. Repairing the error requires keeping speaker and sample scope separate, not merely weakening “everyone” to an equally invented count.

check.subject: reading
choices: Only after the June meeting ended
Before participants submitted any questions
After questions were submitted and before the June meeting
Before the April workshop was announced
check.explanation: The stated sequence is April workshop, submitted questions, revised handout, June meeting. The supported answer is “After questions were submitted and before the June meeting.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The first workshop met in April. Participants submitted questions before a second workshop in June, and the organizers revised the handout for the June meeting using those questions.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: What did the remaining cards directly count?
choices: All seeds passing above the cards
Seeds that struck their surfaces
Every seed leaving the trees
Only seeds later growing into plants
check.explanation: The first sentence defines the measured event, and the second explicitly excludes seeds passing above. The supported answer is “Seeds that struck their surfaces.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The collection cards counted seeds that struck their surfaces. Seeds passing above them were not counted, and two damaged cards were excluded from the report.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: Which condition did the historian state?
choices: Retaining representative fixtures and recording alterations
Keeping dangerous wiring in active use
Removing every old fixture without notes
Closing the building to all visitors forever
check.explanation: The stated support is conditional on retained representative evidence and documentation. The supported answer is “Retaining representative fixtures and recording alterations.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The historian supported replacing dangerous wiring provided that representative old fixtures remained visible and the changes were recorded.

title: Evidence-based inference
intro: Use clues in the passage to reach a supported conclusion.

sections.heading: Use the screen to build a passage map
body: An inference is a conclusion you draw from clues rather than a statement you copy from the text. Look for actions, differences, and limits that support the conclusion.
Keep track of who believes what and what changes. An answer that could happen is not enough; this passage must give reasons to believe it.

examples.label: Worked method: Separate observation from conclusion
examples.text:
When the audience began clapping, Noor remained beside the wings with her program folded in her hand. A loose page lay beneath the last violinist’s chair. While other visitors moved toward the exit, she kept looking at the page.

After the players had left, she crossed the stage and picked it up. Outside, she caught up with the violinist and handed it over without introducing herself or mentioning the applause.

Question: Which inference about Noor’s reason for remaining has the clearest evidentiary link?
A. She wants the audience to recognize her role in the performance.
B. She remains at least partly so she can return the fallen page.
C. She and the violinist had arranged beforehand for her to collect the page.

Supported answer: She remains at least partly so she can return the fallen page.

Reason: Watching the page while others leave, then retrieving and returning it, supports a practical purpose for staying. The purpose is inferred from linked actions rather than stated directly. Public recognition and a prior arrangement add motives or events without a corresponding clue; at least partly avoids claiming this was her only reason.

sections.heading: Make the smallest supported bridge
body: Connect a specific action or statement to the smallest conclusion it supports. Write the link explicitly: the text says __, so __ follows without an added event or motive.
Ask what the choice would require beyond that link. A moment of interest does not establish a career plan; preserving a useful trial does not prove it will succeed permanently.

examples.label: Worked method: Build a minimal motive from action
examples.text:
The potter packed the cracked trial pieces beside the finished bowls. When her student asked why, she placed the pieces in the order they had come from the kiln and pointed out where each firing had changed. She kept the finished bowls on the other side of the table.

Question:  Her arrangement most reasonably suggests that she wants the student to:
A. follow how the process was adjusted across attempts
B. identify the finished bowl most likely to reproduce an early firing defect
C. decide that the final bowls should be displayed without the discarded trials

Supported answer: follow how the process was adjusted across attempts

Reason: Ordering trials and pointing to changes supports following the process across attempts. Predicting a future defect or separating finished work from its developmental record would require another purpose that is not stated. The inference rests on the organized sequence the potter makes visible.

sections.heading: Distinguish reasonable uncertainty from unsupported possibility
body: Separate “could be true” from “supported here.” Checking an archive’s hours supports planning a visit; it does not establish ownership of the archive.
Ask which specific detail makes the inference reasonable. If the same claim could fit almost any passage on the subject, it needs stronger support.

examples.label: Worked method: Distinguish a supported possibility from an invented one
examples.text:
The archivist requested photographs of the bindings before asking to borrow the books. A note on the loan form said that volumes with loose sewing would need supports during transport.

Question: Which inference needs the least extra information?
A. The archivist already knew every book had loose sewing.
B. The owners had refused an earlier loan request.
C. The archivist was checking what protection the books might need in transit.

Supported answer: The archivist was checking what protection the books might need in transit.

Reason: The request for binding photographs is linked to the stated transport condition. It supports checking possible protection needs, not certainty that every binding is loose. A prior refusal is possible but has no clue here. A good inference has a passage-specific reason, not merely a story that could explain the action.

sections.heading: Infer attitudes from choices and contrasts
body: Combine a person’s words with their choices. Positive language can coexist with a practical reservation; an action can settle which concern matters.
Match direction and strength. Concern about a bridge is neither rejection of a route nor confidence that it is usable. Keep unresolved conditions unresolved.

examples.label: Worked method: Keep both halves of a mixed response
examples.text:
“That route would get us there before sunset,” Amari said. She drew her finger along the thin dotted path, then asked whether the footbridge had reopened after the storm. She put the map back on the table instead of folding it into her bag.

Question: Which attitude is best supported?
A. Determination to reject the route
B. Unreserved confidence that the route is ready
C. Interest in its advantage combined with concern about whether it is usable

Supported answer: Interest in its advantage combined with concern about whether it is usable

Reason: Arriving before sunset is a recognized advantage. Asking about the bridge and leaving the map open show an unresolved condition. Total rejection loses the benefit; unreserved confidence loses the practical concern. An attitude answer must explain the action as well as the positive or negative remark.

sections.heading: Use the contradiction test on tempting options
body: For each remaining choice, ask what would have to be true. Then look for a passage detail that supports or contradicts that requirement.
Approving another trial does not promise permanent service. A choice that preserves uncertainty can fit better than one that sounds decisive.

examples.label: Worked method: Use an explicit counterexample
examples.text:
A critic wrote that Ren’s new exhibition abandoned drawing for sculpture. The catalog listed four sculptures and twelve ink drawings. In an interview Ren said the sculptures began as a way to investigate spaces she had left blank on paper.

Question: Which claim is contradicted?
A. Ren has stopped exhibiting drawings.
B. Ren sees a connection between the two media.
C. The exhibition includes fewer sculptures than drawings.

Supported answer: Ren has stopped exhibiting drawings.

Reason: The twelve cataloged ink drawings directly contradict abandonment of exhibited drawing. The interview supports a connection between media, and four is fewer than twelve. A counterexample defeats a universal or exclusive claim without requiring you to settle every aspect of the artist’s intention.

sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: Link a clue to your conclusion: “The text says __, so I can reasonably conclude __.” The better answer should require fewer details you have to invent.
If neither choice has a clear link, return to the relevant action or contrast instead of inventing an explanation.

examples.label: Worked method: Choose the clue that separates rival motives
examples.text:
Before releasing the family recording, Inez sent a copy to her cousin and asked him to mark any passage he did not want shared. She did not ask him to correct dates or identify voices.

Question: Which clue favors concern about consent over concern about factual accuracy?
A. She makes a copy of the recording.
B. She asks which passages he does not want shared.
C. The recording contains more than one voice.

Supported answer: She asks which passages he does not want shared.

Reason: Marking what may be shared is an action directed at permission. Copying and multiple voices could occur in either a consent check or an accuracy check. The explicit absence of date and identity questions reinforces the distinction. For two plausible motives, choose the clue that predicts one more specifically.

sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: After a miss, name the unsupported leap: motive, certainty, future outcome, or a claim about everyone.
Replace it with a smaller conclusion and cite the action or statement that supports it. Try the same process on new text.

examples.label: Worked method: Repair the unsupported leap
examples.text:
After the demonstration, Eli asked to try the loom with a slower shuttle. The instructor brought one out, and Eli stayed after the scheduled finish to make another strip. A classmate concluded that he had decided to become a professional weaver.

Question:  Which smaller conclusion is supported?
A. Eli has concluded that the demonstration method was ineffective.
B. Eli now intends to replace the instructor’s tools with his own.
C. Eli wanted another opportunity to work with an adjusted tool.

Supported answer: Eli wanted another opportunity to work with an adjusted tool.

Reason: Requesting a slower shuttle and continuing supports another attempt under adjusted conditions. It does not establish that the demonstrated method failed or a plan to replace the tools. The career claim in the prompt adds a future commitment beyond those observed actions.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: Jules’s actions most reasonably suggest a wish to:
choices: end the museum’s use of maps altogether
preserve the original project while broadening the evidence
prove the first interviewees invented their memories
make the second map identical to the first
check.explanation: Keeping and relabeling the first map documents it; inviting absent groups expands participation. The supported answer is “preserve the original project while broadening the evidence.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Jules left the original map on display, added a caption naming its interview group, and invited previously absent neighborhoods to contribute to a second map.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The office most likely believes that:
choices: the promising trend still needs testing under different conditions
the trial has proved year-round demand beyond doubt
summer programs never affect attendance
further observations are unnecessary
check.explanation: Extending the trial while changing the seasonal context shows qualified interest rather than certainty. The supported answer is “the promising trend still needs testing under different conditions.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: After seeing a rise in attendance, the office extended the trial into another season and asked whether riders would use the service when the summer program ended.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: Amira’s response is best described as:
choices: entirely hostile from beginning to end
proof she no longer wants to rehearse
certain that every interruption is beneficial
mixed initially, with later recognition of a useful result
check.explanation: The text combines enjoyment and concern, then supplies one specific benefit without a universal claim. The supported answer is “mixed initially, with later recognition of a useful result.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Amira enjoyed the group’s spontaneous song but worried about the rehearsal time it used. Later she tried a phrase suggested during that exchange and found it helped.

title: Words in context
intro: Use the surrounding sentence to work out a word’s meaning.

sections.heading: Use the screen to build a passage map
body: Locate the target word, then read its sentence and the sentences around it. Note what the word describes or acts on.
Your task is its meaning here. A familiar dictionary meaning can be wrong in this context.

examples.label: Worked method: Find the local object of the word
examples.text:
The geographer described the boundary as “porous.” Workers crossed it daily, families maintained homes on both sides, and merchants followed older routes that did not stop at the official markers. The line remained on the map.

Question: What does “porous” mean here?
A. Drawn with gaps in the printed ink
B. Able to admit movement across it
C. Made of material containing small physical holes

Supported answer: Able to admit movement across it

Reason: The following examples concern people and trade crossing a political line, while the mapped line remains. They support permeability to movement, not damaged printing or physical material. Locate what the adjective describes and use the nearby actions to choose its local sense.

sections.heading: Read the local meaning before recalling the dictionary
body: Before looking at choices, replace the word with a plain phrase. “Guarded wording” in a cautious report means wording that avoids a strong claim.
Substitute each candidate into the sentence. Keep the grammar, meaning, and tone of the original.

examples.label: Worked method: Substitute before accepting a familiar sense
examples.text:
“The evidence will bear that interpretation,” the editor wrote, “but not the stronger claim that the author intended the ending to be comic.” She kept the interpretation and removed the claim about intention.

Question: Which substitute for “bear” preserves the sentence?
A. Support
B. Endure with discomfort
C. Produce as offspring

Supported answer: Support

Reason: The editor permits one interpretation because the evidence can support it, then rejects a stronger inference. “Endure” and “produce” are real senses of bear but do not connect evidence to a justified interpretation. Test the candidate in the actual sentence, including its contrast.

sections.heading: Use nearby contrasts and examples as definitions
body: Look for a contrast, example, or explanation near the word. “Spare rather than ornate” points toward minimal decoration.
Use those clues to narrow the meaning before relying on a remembered definition. Then reread the sentence with your substitute.

examples.label: Worked method: Let the contrast define the word
examples.text:
The first sketch spread ornament over every available edge. In the second, the border was “austere”: one dark line surrounded a wide blank margin. The artist had removed detail without changing the central scene.

Question: Which meaning does the contrast establish?
A. Carelessly unfinished
B. Severely simple
C. Old-fashioned in subject matter

Supported answer: Severely simple

Reason: The change from ornamented edges to a single line and blank margin defines a severe simplicity. The second sketch is deliberate, so unfinished carelessness is unsupported. The central scene does not change, so subject matter does not explain the adjective.

sections.heading: Avoid literal answers to a figurative use
body: Ask whether the word describes a real action or creates a comparison. Filing a list away means storing it. A belief “loosening” means becoming less fixed, not being physically untied.
Identify the object of the action. An unresolved question can “haunt” a project without anything supernatural occurring.

examples.label: Worked method: Read figurative action through its target
examples.text:
The old disagreement “shadowed” the committee’s later meetings. Even when a new proposal concerned another building, members returned to who had been trusted with the earlier plans. The room itself was brighter after renovation.

Question: Which meaning of “shadowed” fits?
A. Blocked light from reaching
B. Followed quietly without being noticed
C. Continued to influence in an unsettling way

Supported answer: Continued to influence in an unsettling way

Reason: The subject is an old disagreement and the result is repeated distrust, so the action is figurative influence. The brightened room explicitly makes literal light a poor fit; open returns to the dispute also exclude unnoticed following. Keep the emotional effect as well as the basic sense of continuing presence.

sections.heading: Verify a substitute against the paragraph’s claim
body: After a substitute fits the sentence, test it against the paragraph’s claim. A “neutral” observation method does not influence the result; the word need not refer to soil acidity.
Reject choices that fit the passage’s general subject but change the local argument.

examples.label: Worked method: Check a meaning against the paragraph
examples.text:
The report called the bridge “sound.” It then described bolts that held their load, joints without visible movement, and a surface needing only a new finish. The engineers recommended painting rather than structural replacement.

Question: Which substitute fits the whole paragraph?
A. Structurally reliable
B. Producing a clear noise
C. Based on a persuasive argument

Supported answer: Structurally reliable

Reason: Bolts, joints, and the painting recommendation all concern physical condition. Structurally reliable fits every part. A noise or an argument can also be sound in another sense, but neither explains why replacement is unnecessary here. A local substitute must survive the paragraph, not just the word in isolation.

sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: Use a two-step check: substitute the candidate, then reread the surrounding claim. Eliminate any choice that changes the writer’s attitude or degree of certainty.
Do not spend time listing every dictionary sense. The sentence and paragraph decide which one applies.

examples.label: Worked method: Settle two plausible neighboring senses
examples.text:
The critic called the new ending “restrained.” The central argument remained sharp, but the actor lowered her voice and let the final gesture finish without a speech. The critic praised the force of what was left unsaid.

Question: Which nearby evidence favors “controlled in expression” over “prevented from acting”?
A. The argument remains central.
B. The actor chooses a quieter delivery and ends without an added speech.
C. The review is published after the performance.

Supported answer: The actor chooses a quieter delivery and ends without an added speech.

Reason: The described delivery is a deliberate limit on expression that the critic praises, not an inability to act. A central argument could occur in either kind of performance, and publication timing does not define the word. Identify the feature on which the two possible senses differ.

sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: After a vocabulary miss, record the contextual clue you overlooked: contrast, example, object, or tone.
Write a new sentence using that meaning. Then test the method with a different word in a fresh passage.

examples.label: Worked method: Repair a subject-based dictionary guess
examples.text:
A student reading about a river chose “deposit of money” for “bank.” The sentence read: “The surveyors followed the bank until the reeds hid the water, then returned along a higher ridge.”

Question: Which repair uses the contextual clue?
A. The river must run beside a financial business.
B. Bank means the bordering land, as shown by the route beside reeds and water.
C. Bank means a stored supply of reeds.

Supported answer: Bank means the bordering land, as shown by the route beside reeds and water.

Reason: The route runs beside water and is contrasted with a higher ridge, so the word names bordering land. Financial deposit is familiar but unsupported; a stored supply does not fit a route to follow. Repair the guess by naming the clue that rules in the local meaning rather than memorizing another isolated definition.

check.subject: reading
choices: open to revision
guaranteed to be exact
kept secret permanently
unrelated to evidence
check.explanation: The explanation after the colon directly establishes that the estimate can change with measurements. The supported answer is “open to revision.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The report called the first estimate provisional: the team would revise it as new measurements arrived.

check.subject: reading
choices: inaudible
recently invented
deliberately false
relevant
check.explanation: The contrast links usefulness to the particular research question. The supported answer is “relevant.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The chair movement was distracting to a listener studying pitch, but pertinent to a historian studying the audience’s behavior.

check.subject: reading
choices: was entirely forgotten
became physically larger
became less strict
was tied more tightly
check.explanation: The change affects a rigid belief, and the continuing careful work rules out total abandonment. The supported answer is “became less strict.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Her rigid idea of rehearsal loosened after she saw that careful work could include questions and laughter.

title: Purpose, tone, and structure
intro: Notice how the writer’s choices shape the passage.

sections.heading: Use the screen to build a passage map
body: Map what each paragraph does, not just its topic: introduces a claim, illustrates it, raises an objection, or limits a conclusion.
Track changes in speaker and perspective. A quoted opinion may be included so the author can challenge it.

examples.label: Worked method: Map structure before naming a function
examples.text:
The new mountain road appears as one continuous line joining the coastal town to the villages above it. At the opening, a council speaker called that line a connection for every home.

Rafi could drive his empty cart along the road, but with a full load of grain he stopped at its steepest turn. He carried several sacks around the bend before bringing the cart through.

A map can record a connection without showing the effort it demands from particular users. For Rafi, the road’s usefulness still depends on the cart’s load and the slope beneath its wheels.

Question:  Which structural map fits?
A. Claim about connection → concrete difficulty → qualification of what connection means
B. General claim about travel → proof that the road has no useful purpose → a replacement route
C. A farmer’s difficulty → an account of why he caused it → confirmation of the opening claim

Supported answer: Claim about connection → concrete difficulty → qualification of what connection means

Reason: The farmer’s difficulty links a broad connection claim to the final qualification about usable access. The passage does not reject all usefulness or blame the farmer. Name how the middle changes the opening rather than restating its topic.

sections.heading: Ask what a paragraph does, not only what it says
body: Ask what the detail contributes to the surrounding argument. A commuter’s account can illustrate an access problem without proving that every resident has it.
Connect the paragraph to what comes before and after. A function answer describes that relationship, not merely the detail’s subject.

examples.label: Worked method: Explain why this detail is here
examples.text:
The miniature ship rewards a close look. Its maker carved not only the railings and rigging but also a latch inside a cupboard that visitors cannot open. That hidden fitting extends the precision of the model beyond anything the display ordinarily allows its audience to see.

Question: What is the latch detail’s main function?
A. To show why the cupboard should be opened for visitors
B. To give a concrete instance of workmanship extending beyond visible display
C. To identify a defect that weakens the claim of precision

Supported answer: To give a concrete instance of workmanship extending beyond visible display

Reason: The surrounding claim concerns precision beyond public sight, and the hidden latch exemplifies it. The essay neither requests access nor identifies a defect. Function connects a detail to the argument it supports; it is different from describing the object the detail mentions.

sections.heading: Separate tone from topic and intensity
body: Identify tone from the writer’s wording and treatment of evidence. Approval plus a stated limit supports a cautiously favorable tone.
Match both direction and intensity. A passage about damage can still be measured; one dramatic word does not make the entire passage alarmed.

examples.label: Worked method: Match tone by direction and intensity
examples.text:
This translation is an inviting beginning. Its clear opening gives a new reader room to follow the speaker without losing the abruptness of her questions.

Some later images, however, have become flatter. The small, sharp thing in the original sometimes becomes a broad word for brightness or movement. Those choices smooth the voice where its particularity matters.

I hope a later edition returns to these images. The clarity achieved here makes that next attention worth wanting, rather than making it unnecessary.

Question: Which tone fits the treatment as a whole?
A. Dismissive of the translation’s usefulness
B. Confident that no revision is needed
C. Appreciative but constructively dissatisfied with some choices

Supported answer: Appreciative but constructively dissatisfied with some choices

Reason: “Inviting” and praise establish appreciation; the criticism and requested return establish dissatisfaction with specific choices. Dismissal ignores the praise, while complete satisfaction ignores a full paragraph and the closing wish. Tone must match both the evaluation’s direction and its measured intensity.

sections.heading: Track perspective, quotation, and structural shifts
body: The author writes the piece; the narrator tells the story; a quoted speaker gives their own words. Check who is speaking before deciding whose belief a sentence expresses.
Read what follows a quotation. The author may answer an objection, explain a limit, or compare it with evidence instead of agreeing with it.

examples.label: Worked method: Separate the quoted claim from the author’s response
examples.text:
“Machines have made the hand unnecessary,” a manufacturer announced at the fair. His advertisement showed the finished product sliding from a bright metal opening.

Behind the display, a worker paused the machine when its printed guide failed. She adjusted the feed wheel by touch, ran a test, and adjusted it again before allowing the product to continue.

The hand had not disappeared from this process. Which kinds of handwork, then, had the advertisement taught its visitors not to notice?

Question: Why does the essay include the manufacturer’s claim?
A. To introduce a position that the following observations complicate
B. To certify the claim as the essay’s own conclusion
C. To establish that the workers refused to use the machine

Supported answer: To introduce a position that the following observations complicate

Reason: The quoted assertion is followed by counterevidence: workers still use touch. The final question directly examines the advertisement’s framing. Quotation does not equal endorsement, and adjustment is not refusal to use the machine. Follow what the author does after another speaker’s words.

sections.heading: Explain the effect of imagery without overreading it
body: Name the feature an image carries across: light against darkness, stillness against movement, or closeness against distance. Then connect that feature to the surrounding scene or argument.
Do not import every property of the comparison object. A greenhouse compared with moons can evoke pale light without making an astronomical claim.

examples.label: Worked method: Explain an image’s selected relationship
examples.text:
At dusk the greenhouse panes became “a row of small moons” above the dark garden. Inside, workers moved seedlings from tray to tray; outside, the path had disappeared into shadow.

Question:  What does the image chiefly emphasize?
A. The reflection of actual moonlight onto the workers
B. A separated line of pale light against surrounding darkness
C. A match between the workers’ movements and the regular spacing of the panes

Supported answer: A separated line of pale light against surrounding darkness

Reason: The shared feature is a row of pale lights against darkness, reinforced by the shadowed path. The image does not identify the physical source as moonlight or align the workers’ movements with the panes. Explain the selected visual relationship rather than adding another part of the scene.

sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: For a purpose question, read the sentence with its neighbors. Name what it does: gives an example, questions a claim, adds a limit, or shows a difference.
For tone, compare two pieces of wording. Reject choices that overstate the emotion or confuse the topic with the attitude.

examples.label: Worked method: Distinguish example, concession, and reversal
examples.text:
I want the old stairway to remain available. It is narrow, and carrying boxes up it is awkward. But the new side entrance can handle deliveries while the stair stays open for ordinary use. Preserving it need not require pretending that every task belongs on it.

Question: What does the admission do?
A. It withdraws the argument for keeping the stairs.
B. It supplies the main benefit of the old design.
C. It acknowledges a practical objection that the proposed arrangement addresses.

Supported answer: It acknowledges a practical objection that the proposed arrangement addresses.

Reason: The inconvenience is a concession, not the author’s reason for preservation. The next sentence offers an answer without reversing the position. Use the neighboring sentences to distinguish an acknowledged problem from abandonment of the claim.

sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: After a miss, name what you mixed up: what a detail says versus why it is there, a quoted speaker versus the author, an actual fact versus an image, or a mild feeling versus an extreme one.
Explain why the writer placed the detail there, then apply the same distinction to a new passage.

examples.label: Worked method: Repair a purpose answer that only retells
examples.text:
Before leaving, I checked the forecast three times. The same chance of showers remained on the screen; I wanted a more cooperative answer. I finally put the phone away and hurried toward the club.

When rain began, I kept going. By the time I arrived, my sleeves were wet, my shoes made a noise on the floor, and I was laughing.

A student labels the first paragraph’s purpose “to tell us that the narrator checks the weather.”

Question: Which revision explains its role rather than repeating its content?
A. It establishes a wish for control, against which the later response becomes a change.
B. It establishes the checks as evidence that the later rain was forecast accurately.
C. It shows why reaching the club depends on obtaining a different forecast.

Supported answer: It establishes a wish for control, against which the later response becomes a change.

Reason: Wanting a more cooperative forecast supplies evidence of a wish for a manageable outcome; later laughter in the rain changes that response. The task is not to establish forecast accuracy or a condition for reaching the club. Connecting the first paragraph to the later response explains its role rather than merely repeating the weather-checking action.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The festival detail mainly serves to:
choices: prove the attendance count was fabricated
explain why every resident opposes the route
show that further trials are impossible
qualify what the attendance increase can establish
check.explanation: The detail introduces a simultaneous influence that limits interpretation of the increase. The supported answer is “qualify what the attendance increase can establish.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Attendance increased during the trial. Yet the report noted that a festival took place at the same time and recommended another trial after the festival ended.

check.subject: reading
choices: why the singer never performed live
why all digital copies must be identical
why different sounds require different processing judgments
why every rough sound should be removed
check.explanation: The contrast concerns confidence about each sound’s source and the resulting restoration choice. The supported answer is “why different sounds require different processing judgments.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: The engineer compared a surface click with the singer’s rough vocal edge. One could confidently be attributed to the recording medium; the other might belong to the performance.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: The changing chair arrangements primarily reveal:
choices: an unchanged preference for appearances above use
a shift toward practical needs and shared use
a decision to end all musical work
evidence that every chair is damaged
check.explanation: The three arrangements trace a movement from image to function and acceptance of other room purposes. The supported answer is “a shift toward practical needs and shared use.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: At first the narrator arranged chairs symmetrically to make the room look serious. Later the narrator moved them to help the players see one another, then returned them for a family visit.

title: Paired texts and visual evidence
intro: Connect ideas across passages and compare their evidence.

sections.heading: Use the screen to build a passage map
body: Map each source separately before combining them. Write a short claim for A and a separate claim for B, including each condition or limit.
For a graphic, read its title, labels, units, and time period. Similar-looking numbers may measure different things.

examples.label: Worked method: Map each claim before finding overlap
examples.text:
Source A: The new route shortens the walk from the station to the clinic. Its value is the direct connection it creates.

Source B: A shorter walk helps only if people can use the surface throughout the year. I support the route, but its drainage must be funded as part of construction.

Question:  Which two-column map is faithful?
A. A: connection matters; B: connection matters with a maintained-surface condition
B. A: a direct route matters only after drainage is funded; B: a shorter walk is sufficient by itself
C. A: the clinic’s distance is irrelevant; B: the drainage question should be postponed until after construction

Supported answer: A: connection matters; B: connection matters with a maintained-surface condition

Reason: A emphasizes a shorter connection. B accepts its benefit but requires drainage to be part of the construction plan. The wrong maps transfer a condition to the wrong writer, reverse its force, or remove the benefit A actually stresses.

sections.heading: Map each source before comparing them
body: Compare each writer’s claim and conditions. A director may support safe renovation while a historian supports it only if representative evidence survives.
Name both the shared aim and the difference. Do not turn a condition from one writer into a demand made by both.

examples.label: Worked method: Retain the precise difference between supporters
examples.text:
Writer A supports publishing the letters so readers can encounter the correspondence directly. Writer B also supports publication, provided the edition identifies missing pages and distinguishes uncertain dates from confirmed ones. Neither argues for rewriting the letters.

Question:  Where do the positions differ?
A. Whether publishing the letters is useful without any new research about their authors
B. Whether a complete-looking edition is preferable to one that marks its gaps
C. B explicitly requires documentation of gaps and uncertain dates.

Supported answer: B explicitly requires documentation of gaps and uncertain dates.

Reason: Both support publication. B explicitly adds documentation of missing pages and uncertain dates; the text does not establish an opposing preference by A for concealment. The distinction is a stated condition, not an invented disagreement inferred from A’s silence.

sections.heading: Combine evidence without inventing a compromise
body: A combined conclusion must be supported by the supplied sources. Put their claims together without inventing a compromise.
“The pilot improved access” and “its costs remain uncertain” can both be true. Neither statement proves that any cost is worthwhile.

examples.label: Worked method: Combine compatible claims without inventing a verdict
examples.text:
A landscape study reports that the planted strip reduced wind speed at the field edge. A second report finds that the strip occupies land previously used for crops, but does not calculate the value of either the lost crop area or the wind protection.

Question: Which joint conclusion follows?
A. The protection is worth more than the lost crop area.
B. The strip provides measured wind protection while the overall economic tradeoff remains uncalculated.
C. The loss of crop area cancels the measured wind reduction.

Supported answer: The strip provides measured wind protection while the overall economic tradeoff remains uncalculated.

Reason: The sources establish a physical benefit and a cost in land use, not their relative economic values. They can both be true without canceling one another. A combined answer may retain an unresolved tradeoff; it must not create a cost-benefit verdict absent from either source.

sections.heading: Read the graphic’s labels before its pattern
body: Keep quantities and denominators consistent. Eighty-one on-time returns out of ninety scheduled returns is 90%; eighty-one alone is a count.
Occupied seats and unique visitors measure different things. Check definitions before treating a graph as evidence for the passage’s claim.

examples.label: Worked method: Read the table’s unit before making the claim
examples.text:
The gallery records each doorway entry, including a person returning after leaving.

Day — Doorway entries
Friday — 120
Saturday — 150

A companion note explains that workshop participants often left for lunch and returned through the same doors. The table therefore counts entry events rather than assigning a new identity to each event.

Question: Which claim uses both the table and definition correctly?
A. The gallery had thirty more distinct visitors on Saturday.
B. Twenty-five percent of Saturday visitors attended the workshop.
C. Saturday had thirty more entries, but the figures do not identify the change in distinct visitors.

Supported answer: Saturday had thirty more entries, but the figures do not identify the change in distinct visitors.

Reason: Subtract like units: 150 − 120 = 30 entries. Repeat entry means that difference is not automatically thirty new people. Workshop behavior explains a possible difference between measures but gives no percentage of visitors. Both the numeric operation and the unit definition must survive the combined claim.

sections.heading: Keep a combined conclusion within all supplied limits
body: Check a proposed conclusion against every source’s limits. Fewer requests blocked by overdue tools does not mean every requested tool was available.
A conclusion about two tested groups does not establish all groups or equal effects. Preserve who was measured and under which conditions.

examples.label: Worked method: Respect the intersection of study limits
examples.text:
Study A found improved recall for adults learning short lists aloud. Study B found improved recall for teenagers practicing pictures silently. Neither study compared the two methods in the same participants, and neither measured retention after a week.

Question: Which combined conclusion stays inside both studies?
A. A benefit occurred under each tested method and group, without establishing which method lasts longer.
B. Speaking is equally effective for adults and teenagers.
C. The two studies prove that both methods preserve learning for a week.

Supported answer: A benefit occurred under each tested method and group, without establishing which method lasts longer.

Reason: A and B each support a benefit in their own tested conditions. Different groups and materials prevent assigning their difference solely to method, and neither measures week-long retention. Combining positive results does not erase limits, create an age comparison, or supply an unmeasured time period.

sections.heading: Pace a decision instead of rereading everything
body: Build a two-column comparison in your head: A claims __; B claims __. Locate the exact overlap or disagreement the question asks about.
For a graph or table, read the needed row or point and connect it to the passage. Do not assume two things are related just because they look similar.

examples.label: Worked method: Use the exact point of disagreement
examples.text:
Historian A treats a merchant’s list as a record of goods intended for shipment. Historian B agrees about that purpose but warns that the list alone does not establish which goods arrived; she asks to compare a receiving ledger.

Question:  Which evidence would most directly address B’s additional question?
A. A second copy confirming which goods the merchant intended to send
B. A ledger identifying the goods received at the destination
C. A ledger showing what similar merchants sent to other destinations

Supported answer: A ledger identifying the goods received at the destination

Reason: B asks which goods arrived in this shipment. Another plan confirms intention, and other merchants’ records provide a comparison without documenting this delivery. The receiving ledger addresses the precise step B wants checked.

sections.heading: Review the reason for the miss and test the repair
body: After a miss, identify whether you merged speakers, ignored a condition, changed units, or claimed more than both sources support.
Repair the combined claim in one sentence and verify it against each source separately. Then try a fresh pair of sources.

examples.label: Worked method: Repair a merged-speaker conclusion
examples.text:
A designer says the square should retain its old benches because people recognize them as meeting places. A wheelchair user supports retaining some, but asks for spaces beside them wide enough for different seating needs. A summary says both oppose changing the bench area.

Question: Which repair preserves both positions?
A. Both think recognition is the only important consideration.
B. The wheelchair user rejects retaining any old benches.
C. Both allow old benches to remain, while the wheelchair user also calls for changes around them.

Supported answer: Both allow old benches to remain, while the wheelchair user also calls for changes around them.

Reason: Retaining benches is the overlap; changing adjacent space is the added condition. The mistaken summary turns agreement about an object into agreement against every alteration. Repair by naming each speaker’s actual scope instead of treating all support for preservation as opposition to change.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: Which claim would both writers most likely accept?
choices: Only the smoothest version should survive
Future listeners must ask today’s exact questions
A useful listening copy should be accompanied by access to evidence about its production
All processing is inherently unacceptable
check.explanation: A asks for inspectable changes; B asks for retained copies and notes. Both support usable presentations with evidence preserved. The supported answer is “A useful listening copy should be accompanied by access to evidence about its production.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context:
Passage A: A restored recording should be easier to hear, but listeners should be able to inspect changes.

Passage B: Public listening copies are useful, but institutions should retain original copies and notes so later researchers can ask different questions.

check.subject: reading
choices: The number of scheduled returns stayed the same
The on-time proportion increased, but the reminder’s separate effect is not isolated
The increase proves reminders alone caused every change
The later on-time proportion was 45 percent
check.explanation: The proportions are60percent and75percent; the simultaneous hours change limits causal attribution. The supported answer is “The on-time proportion increased, but the reminder’s separate effect is not isolated.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Before a reminder trial, 30 of 50 scheduled returns were on time. During the trial, 45 of 60 were on time. The report notes that opening hours also changed.

check.subject: reading
check.questionText: How does B’s position relate to A’s?
choices: It shares support for use while adding conditions about historical evidence
It denies that anyone should enter the theater
It proves that every old mechanism is safe
It treats documentation as a replacement for all surviving features
check.explanation: B agrees about continued use and adds retained mechanisms plus documentation; that is a qualification, not total opposition. The supported answer is “It shares support for use while adding conditions about historical evidence.” Reject choices that change the stated facts, exceed the evidence, or answer a different question.

passage.title: Quick check passage
passage.context: Passage A argues that public use helps a theater survive. Passage B supports continued use but asks that representative old stage mechanisms remain visible and alterations be documented.
